title: Lipids First
author: Perri Thaler
dek: Compartments arrive before genes. Chemistry learns to stay in one place.

sections.heading: A room before a recipe
sections.body:
PLACEHOLDER — full paragraph(s) go here verbatim from doc.

Fatty-acid vesicles form spontaneously. They grow. They divide. They keep a inside and an outside. In the lipid-first telling, that is not a late luxury — it is the opening move. Without a room, chemistry is a river. With a room, a reaction can persist when the tide changes.

The vesicles do not need a genome to be interesting. They need a supply of amphiphiles, a wet-dry cycle or a shear, and a reason for one bubble to outlast another.

sections.heading: Inheritance without a gene
sections.body:
PLACEHOLDER — full paragraph(s) go here verbatim from doc.

Some researchers argue that composition itself can be hereditary: the mix of lipids in a membrane is a kind of memory. Others say a compartment is only useful once something inside it starts to copy.

This piece is the case for rooms first — and the holes in that case, which the closer will press on.
